I don't normally engage with the "What right do you have?" crowd. A fairer question would be "Why don't you favor legalization?" I'd gladly answer that because that is a question from someone who is interested in discussion and who recognizes at least that I have a right to express my position on the issue. "What right do you have?" is a question from someone whose mind is shut off from other possibilities or ideas besides his own.

But rather than cause you to think I'm dodging the issue entirely, I'll answer both questions.

First, the reason I don't favor legalization is that I don't want it openly accepted and endorsed in my community. I don't want weed culture in my neighborhood, and I don't want my kids exposed to it. I don't care what people do in their own homes away from the public eye, and I don't want police breaking down people's doors because the neighbors smelled weed. That's where it belongs--in private. I don't want my neighbor cutting his grass naked either, but I don't care if he hangs out naked in his living room.

There's a whole host of responses that come after an argument like the above, one of which is the alcohol question: "What about alcohol?" When talking about controlled substances, individuals, society, and government have an obligation to weigh each one independently. While alcohol can get you drunk, the purpose of a drink--for most people--is not to get drunk. The same cannot be said of marijuana. It can get you high, and the purpose of a joint--for most people--is to get high. So I reject the comparison. It's a different issue entirely. They're not analogous.

Another question that comes up is, "Why not legalize it, regulate it, and tax it?" While government coffers would probably grow initially, we all know what would happen. Increased use would cause some bright young legislator (probably on the left) to decide that people need the government to closely watch, regulate, and control marijuana use. This would give rise to new bureaucracies and new expenditures, depleting those new funds in no time, after which that revenue would have to be found elsewhere--time to raise taxes. And the cycle continues as it always does. Thanks, but no.

Finally, I'll get to your actual question, distasteful though it is to me. What right do I have to control what people do with their own bodies? The truth is that I don't want to. I don't care what they do with their bodies. I care what they do with my community. And it is my right, as it is yours and everyone else's, to advocate for laws that I think make a better community. If I don't like the laws that exist, then it's also my right to promote better ideas and to encourage the community to change or repeal the laws to which I object. This is the system in which we live, and while it's not perfect, I think it's better than the alternatives. So I don't need to defend my rights against sanctimonious rhetoric. We have the same rights, my friend. Our opinions differ. If you don't like mine, then convince enough people to agree with you and change the law.
